title: The hills
hookLine: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills (Psalm 121)
tomorrow: Jonah ran to the edge of the map. what was waiting there?

cards: Up a switchback, legs burning, somebody stops and looks at the ridge: how much farther? An old song starts right there. In the King James Bible, Psalm 121 carries the heading "A Song of degrees," a song of going up.

Deuteronomy tells the men of Israel to come before the LORD three times a year, at the feasts, in the place he would choose, and some readers hear these songs as walking songs for that climb to Jerusalem.
So: a family on the road, packs on their backs, hills on every side. And somebody looks up.

teach.b: Here's the first line. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." Hold it there.
On that road the hills are beautiful, and they're also where trouble hides. So the line can hang in the air like a question: where does my help come from? From those hills?

teach.h: THE MAKER OF HEAVEN AND EARTH.
teach.b: "My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth." The eyes go up to the hills. The help comes from past them, from the one who made the hills.
Then the psalm turns to the walker and starts making promises.
"Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep." The pilgrim will have to sleep by the road tonight. The keeper won't.
The word keeps coming back, verse after verse: "The LORD is thy keeper."
And the last promise covers the whole trip: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore."
Leaving, and coming home, both kept. That's the teaching Jews and Christians take from this psalm: God as the keeper of the traveler, awake when they can't be.
It's why some people pray it before a trip, or by a hospital bed. And it's a move you can borrow: look up at what's big, then name where help really comes from.

how: Psalm 121 is prayed by Jews and Christians; some say it before a journey or at a sickbed, and its last verse, about going out and coming in, is used as a blessing for travelers.

o: the high places a traveler must avoid on the road
the holy mountains where ancient Israel's gods lived
where a pilgrim looks up before naming the maker as help

games.q: the walker's psalm: tap the pairs.
p: the maker of heaven and earth

s: Psalm 121 says your help comes from the hills
the eyes go to the hills; the next line says help comes from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
the psalm's last promise covers both leaving and coming home
"thy going out and thy coming in," from this time forth.
in the psalm, the keeper rests when the traveler rests
he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.

games.q: a friend is scared the night before a long solo drive across the country. which part of Psalm 121 speaks to the night?
o: the keeper who shall neither slumber nor sleep.
the hills themselves, which will watch over the road.
the view: look up at the scenery and the fear will pass.
games.why: the psalm's answer to a night on the road is a keeper who stays awake, and a promise over the going out and the coming in.

practice: Look up now at the highest thing in view: a hill out a window, a roofline, a treetop, or just the sky. Keep your eyes there and let your breath slow down.
Then ask the psalm's question under your breath, from whence cometh my help, and let its next line answer.

wordCard.voice: The hills: where the psalm singer looks first, before he names the maker of heaven and earth as his help.

orig.note: Hebrew, Psalm 121:1: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills.

carryVoice: Keep this: lift up mine eyes, and then say where the help comes from. A new week of psalms, and the road goes up.
